subject: Archaeology
title: The Library of Ashurbanipal
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Library of Ashurbanipal.

hook.text: An Assyrian king built the world's first organized library — 30,000 clay tablets covering everything from medicine to math.

buildup.text: Ashurbanipal sent scribes across his empire to copy every text they could find. He wanted all knowledge in one place.

discovery.text: Layard found the library at Nineveh in 1852. The tablets had survived because fire baked the clay, preserving them.

twist.text: The library held the only complete copy of the Epic of Gilgamesh.

climax.text: The tablets are still being translated today. Thousands remain unread in museum basements — unknown stories waiting.

punchline.text: A tyrant saved the world's oldest literature.

quiz.question: How were Ashurbanipal's clay tablets accidentally preserved?
options: They were sealed in waterproof jars before the city fell
The fire that destroyed Nineveh baked the clay tablets, making them permanent
Scribes had coated them in a preservative resin before storage

details.summary: King Ashurbanipal of Assyria assembled the ancient world's first systematically organized library at Nineveh around 650 BCE. Over 30,000 clay tablets covered literature, science, medicine, magic, and law — including the only complete copy of the Epic of Gilgamesh.
details.whyItMatters: Ashurbanipal's library preserved Mesopotamian knowledge that would otherwise be lost. Its discovery gave modern scholars access to over two millennia of accumulated learning from a civilization that had been almost entirely forgotten.
takeaways: Ashurbanipal built the first organized library around 650 BCE
Over 30,000 tablets covered literature, science, magic, and law
The library preserved the complete Epic of Gilgamesh

faq.question: How was the Library of Ashurbanipal discovered?
faq.answer: Austen Henry Layard and his assistant Hormuzd Rassam excavated Nineveh in the 1850s, uncovering rooms packed with clay tablets. The tablets were shipped to the British Museum, where scholars slowly deciphered their contents over the following decades.

faq.question: What kinds of texts were in the library?
faq.answer: Everything from epic poetry and divination texts to medical prescriptions, astronomical observations, mathematical tables, and diplomatic correspondence. The collection was comprehensive, suggesting Ashurbanipal sought to preserve all known Mesopotamian knowledge.
